elements.note: A soft-mutated form of mab 'son'; ab is used before vowels, and it fused into surnames such as Powell and Bowen.
In names the soft-mutated ferch means 'daughter of', the female match for ap.
Gwen is the feminine form, and is also a given name in its own right.
Cognate with Gaelic dubh.
Borrowed early from Latin coccum 'scarlet berry'.
A nickname for someone with grey hair; Lloyd and Floyd are English spellings.
Bychan, a diminutive of bach, became the surname Vaughan; cognate with Gaelic beag.
Shows up after the noun in place names, often softened to -fawr.
Comes before the noun, as in hendre, the lowland home farm (SNSBI).
Covers the crow family generally, including rook and raven.
Some Welsh rivers are named from animals: the Arth and the Twrch 'wild boar' (SNSBI).
Plural bleiddiau.
Borrowed from Latin leo.
Also used in Pictish, as in Aberdeen 'mouth of the Don'.

examples.name: Abercynon
examples.gloss: where the Cynon meets the Taf

elements.note: Usually followed by a saint's name, which softens (Mair becomes -fair).
Borrowed from Latin ecclesia.
Borrowed from Old English bedhūs 'prayer house'.
Often appears as Tre- or Dre-; compare Old English tūn.
Often used of old Roman forts, much like English -chester.
From din 'fort', which survives in Tenby (Dinbych 'little fort').
Used of hilltops, headlands and the ends of things.
Borrowed into English as coomb.
Cognate with Gaelic gleann.
In older names it can also mean the valley of a stream.
Source of the English river name Avon.
Not the same word as the peninsula Llŷn.
One of several Welsh words for a hill, with bre, moel and mynydd.

examples.name: Mynydd Epynt
examples.gloss: upland crossed by a horse path

elements.note: Related to Gaelic and Irish ros, which means a promontory or wood.
Cognate with Irish inis.
Borrowed from Latin pons.
Two words share this spelling: porth 'harbour' and porth 'gateway'.
Irish baile 'townland, town' is the most common Irish place-name word, as Bally-. Not every Bal- is baile (Balloch is bealach 'pass').

examples.name: Baile Átha Cliath
examples.gloss: town of the ford of hurdles (Dublin)

elements.note: The Gaelic match for Brittonic aber; Ayr and Nairn once had Inver- spellings.
Irish has binn or beann 'peak, cliff'.
Irish srath means river meadow; Strathclyde is from the Brittonic cousin of this word.
The same word in Irish; Welsh glyn is a cousin.
Irish loch (anglicised Lough) means lake or inlet.
Irish has oileán; inis is an older word for island.
In Irish place names allt or alt means a steep-sided glen, height or cliff.
Irish achadh, also 'field', mostly survives only in place names.
Irish mór is the same word; both usually follow the noun as -more.
Used the same way in Irish surnames; cognate with Welsh mab.
Short for nighean mhic; used by women in place of Mac in both Gaelic and Irish.
Modern Irish spells it rua; Welsh rhudd is a cousin.
Irish bán also means lea-ground, grassy land, in place names.
The second half of Donnchadh (Duncan) is disputed: 'battle' or 'noble'.
Same word in Irish; Welsh gwyn is a cousin. Fiona was popularised in the 1700s.
Scottish Gaelic dùn 'fortification, fortified hill' gives Dundee and Dunfermline; Welsh din, dinas is a cousin.
Borrowed from Latin cella; just as common in Scottish Gaelic, usually with a saint's name.
Also used in Scottish Gaelic for a hillock or knoll.
Scottish Gaelic druim, the same word.
Scottish Gaelic has àird 'height, point, promontory'.
Same word in Scottish Gaelic; Welsh carreg is a cousin.
Scottish Gaelic innis 'small island, meadow' gives Inch- names; Welsh ynys is a cousin.
Also Scottish Gaelic; compare Welsh rhos 'moor'.
Older spelling magh, also used in Scottish Gaelic.
Scottish Gaelic àth 'ford' too.

elements.note: An earthen ring-fort, very common in Irish townland names.
Same word in Scottish Gaelic; Welsh du is a cousin.
Same word in Scottish Gaelic; Welsh bach is a cousin.
Covers green-blue-grey shades. Glasgow is from the Brittonic cousin: 'green hollow' (SNSBI).
Anglicised as O'; women use Ní instead.
Short for iníon uí, from iníon 'daughter'; the women's form of Ó.
